title: Privileged Remote Access Credential Agent Deployment Guide

blocks.text: Privileged Remote Access (PRA) Credential Management uses a credential agent to establish connectivity with Active Directory (AD) or Microsoft Entra. For credential management operations, a dedicated App Connector is required. The Zscaler cloud communicates with the App Connector using mutual TLS (mTLS). The App Connector then establishes a separate, dedicated mTLS connection to the credential agent to interface with Active Directory or Microsoft Entra. Private Access (ZPA) can communicate with the credential agent over HTTPS.

Create and name all certificates in accordance with corporate standard operating procedures, referencing the provided examples. Export the Active Directory (AD) Root CA certificate in PEM or DER format, and install it into the credential agent operating system's trust store.

blocks.item: Step 1: Make Sure You Have Met the Prerequisites
Before you begin any procedures within this guide, make sure that you have the following:
Active Directory (LDAPS) prerequisites
Active Directory Domain Service (AD DS) must support LDAPS (TCP/636).
The AD server certificate must be valid.

The AD service account for the credential agent to reset the password in Active Directory. The service account name must follow a purpose-based naming standard like svc-credagent-bind. The service account must have the following settings applied:
Account enable: Yes
Password: Long, random, non-human password
Password expiration: Disabled or externally managed
User can change password: Disabled
Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated: Enabled
Privileged group membership: Prohibited

Group-based delegation must be created and assigned. Permissions must be assigned to security groups, not directly to service accounts. You must have a service account as a member of the group. Group-based delegation must have the following settings applied:
Delegation Permission: Reset Password (Extended rights)
Delegation Scope:
Applied on: OU=<Business Unit OU>
Applies to: Descendant User objects
Explicitly prohibited permissions:
Full Control
GenericAll
Write All Properties
Domain-wide delegation
App Connector prerequisites

Before deploying an App Connector on any supported platform, Zscaler highly recommends reading the following information and making the necessary changes to your organization's environment, where applicable.
App Connector Specifications and Sizing Requirements
App Connector Platform Prerequisites
App Connector Security Guidance and Firewall Requirements
After you have met all the prerequisites, you can deploy the App Connector on a supported platform.
The following specifications are recommended by Zscaler for each App Connector:
Memory: 4 GB RAM

For Digital Experience (ZDX) deployments, Zscaler recommends App Connectors to have 8 GB of RAM. If the ZDX probes exceed a count of 2,000 at an interval of 5 minutes, further scaling should be considered. If alerts are observed that exceed a configured bandwidth of 250 Mbps on each App Connector, further scaling of 32 GB of RAM should be considered.
CPU:
2 CPU cores (Xeon E5 class) for physical machines without hyperthreading
4 CPU cores (Xeon E5 class) for virtual machines (VMs) with hyperthreading
Both Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) require a minimum of 4 CPU cores due to hyperthreading.
To deploy an App Connector on AWS, Zscaler recommends using t3.xlarge (for non-production or low traffic App Connectors) or m5a.xlarge (for production or high traffic App Connectors).
To deploy an App Connector on GCP, Zscaler recommends using a Linux RPM on n2-standard-4 or n2-highcpu-4.
Azure VMs older than V3 require 2 CPU cores, while VMs V3 and later require 4 CPU cores due to hyperthreading.
To deploy an App Connector on Azure, Zscaler recommends using Standard_D4s_v4 or Standard_D4s_v5 or later.

To enable AppProtection using the default AppProtection profile provided by Zscaler, we recommend that your App Connectors have at least 8 CPU cores and 8 GB of memory. Ensure that your App Connectors are less than 40% for peak memory utilization and peak CPU utilization. If your CPU or memory utilization is above the suggested maximum, you need to add App Connectors to reach the maximum peak of 40% CPU and memory without AppProtection enabled. This rule also applies if you are using a smaller VM (4 CPUs, 4 GB). Your App Connector throughput might be 100 to 200 Mbps depending on App Connector sizing when using AppProtection. Monitor your App Connectors by going to the App Connector dashboard.

The AppProtection recommendations are based on a mix of web traffic, 85% GET requests, and 15% POST and payload and response sizes of 32 KB. Smaller payload and response sizes might require less App Connector resources and result in higher throughput.
For ZDX deployments, Zscaler recommends App Connectors to have 4 CPU cores.

Using the PassMark Software Pty Ltd benchmark to verify the CPU Mark score, Zscaler recommends using a minimum CPU benchmark score of 2640 when choosing a CPU processor. The Intel Advanced Encryption Standard New Instructions (AES-NI) instruction set must also be enabled on the CPU processor.
To learn more, see the App Connector Deployment Guide for your platform.
Disk Space: 64 GB (thin provisioned) for all deployment platforms
Network Card: 1 NIC (minimum)

For VMware platform deployment, the default configuration to allow the host to dynamically allocate VM resources is not recommended. Configure the VM setting to reserve the following memory and CPU allocations:
Memory: 8 GB RAM
CPU: total CPU GHz (the number of cores (2 or 4 cores) multiplied by the GHz per core)
To learn more, refer to the VMware documentation.
For Microsoft Hyper-V deployment, ensure that you have the following:
A physical server with Windows Server 2025 Standard or Datacenter Edition OS virtualization support
Intel VT-x or AMD-V hardware virtualization support
Second Level Address Translation (SLAT) support
Minimum 16 GB RAM (recommended based on VM workload requirements)
Sufficient local storage for Host OS and VM VHDX files
For Microsoft Azure Local deployment, ensure that you have the following:
An HCI cluster that includes:
Windows Admin Center installed
A designated static management network IP address
A node created in the HCI cluster
Servers must be connected to the same network switch and subnet

The management server must be reachable and the DNS role configured before joining the domain. You must have an Active Directory (AD) Domain Services (DS) role for joining cluster nodes to the domain.
Remote Desktop (RDP) access enabled on each server via sconfig

Using these specifications, each App Connector supports up to 500 Mbps of throughput. To learn more, see Understanding App Connector Throughput in this article. Based on Zscaler's recommendations, determine the App Connector sizing requirements for your deployment. If disk space fills up in the App Connector, Zscaler recommends archiving files and creating more log space. To learn more, see Monitoring App Connector Performance.
500 Mbps of throughput is an aggregate of multiple streams of traffic.

After an App Connector is enrolled, an outbound TLS tunnel over port 443 is established to the Private Access (ZPA) cloud infrastructure. This communication channel provides various functionality and utilizes minimal bandwidth, which includes the following traffic:
Periodic keepalives to Public Service Edges or Private Service Edges for Private Access
Application learning
Application health reporting
App Connector software upgrades (upgrades are completed based on a weekly schedule)

You can deploy additional App Connectors at any time, using the same provisioning key to add them to the existing App Connector Group, while ensuring network and internet connectivity. App Connectors are designed to scale elastically. You can deploy additional App Connectors in the same App Connector group to increase the total throughput as required by your deployment. Zscaler recommends you have a minimum of two healthy App Connectors to always ensure an available path. To learn more, see About Deploying App Connectors and Supported Platforms for App Connectors.
After deployment, ensure that the App Connector meets your sizing requirements.
Throughput numbers are aggregate (i.e., total inbound and outbound). The following best practices apply regarding App Connector throughput sizing:
Check your existing VPN solution's average and peak throughput. Be sure to only account for user/client VPN traffic and not any site-to-site tunnel traffic.
App Connectors communicate over the provided (default) gateway, which is most likely your ISP WAN broadband connection.
Using double encryption affects throughput. However, the effect varies based on the number of applications that are enabled for double encryption.

If you have a 1 Gbps connection (aggregate) in your data center, you can use the throughput guidelines in the following table to make sure that you have enough App Connectors to support the connection and room for failover (N+1). For example, with a 1 Gbps connection, you would need to deploy 2 to 3 App Connectors if your applications are not using double encryption, but 4 to 6 App Connectors if they are. To learn more, see Understanding Double Encryption.
The following throughput guidelines apply based upon the recommended App Connector specifications:

It is possible to increase App Connector throughput up to 1 Gbps per App Connector by running the App Connector on hardware with more memory and CPUs along with increased network link speed. If you have a 10 Gbps connection (aggregate) in your data center, and you want to increase the App Connector throughput up to 1 Gbps per App Connector, you can increase the underlying VM spec as follows:
8 vCPU cores for virtual machines or 4 CPU cores for physical machines
8 GB RAM

The exact throughput can vary and depends on other network factors such as your internal network setup, latency, and whether you have double encryption, App Protection, or ZDX enabled. Make sure that you have enough App Connectors to support the connection and room for failover (N+1).

Zscaler recommends that you have more App Connectors with lower specifications rather than fewer App Connectors with higher specifications to horizontally scale your deployment. For example, if you have fewer App Connectors with higher specifications and one fails, you could adversely affect more user application traffic or sessions than a smaller App Connector that fails.
Before you begin any procedures within the App Connector Deployment Guide for your platform, make sure that you have the following:
Intel x86_64/AMD64-based architecture
systemd
Root or sudo access to the system to configure a new package repository and install packages
DNS resolution and network access
For OAuth 2.0 enrollment, Manager software and App Connector version 25.46.3 or later

An OAuth 2.0 enrollment token obtained from a hyperscaler marketplace, virtual image, or RPM installer provided by Zscaler, or an App Connector provisioning key obtained from the Zscaler Admin Console
The OAuth server only supports IPv4-based communication. If an App Connector only has an IPv6 address, it cannot access the OAuth server.
A static MAC address

blocks.item: App Connectors can be deployed in different ways (as private cloud VMs, public cloud VMs, or OS packages), so the security features for each deployment type are slightly different.

Zscaler recommends treating access to App Connectors as privileged, so only authorized personnel can access an App Connector's console. By limiting access, there is the added benefit of shielding inter-process communication within the App Connector from attack.

The App Connector VMs distributed by Zscaler for use in private clouds are configured without any remotely accessible services running. Swap partitions are disabled on the App Connector VMs to ensure that memory growth does not have an impact on App Connector performance. For enhanced security, you must use the passwd command to change the credentials on the default admin account. To learn more, see the App Connector Deployment Guide for the platform you're using.

Private Access provides Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) VM images for AWS, GCP, Microsoft Azure, Nutanix, and VMware by default. To learn more, see App Connector Software by Platform. The remaining private and public cloud VM images provided by Zscaler are configured with minimal listening services to reduce the remotely exploitable attack surface. Because these are essentially unmodified operating systems (currently based on RHEL 9.x), you can patch these systems when necessary by using the standard yum OS update mechanism. Zscaler recommends that you harden the operating system, including the sshd-config file, on the VM images in accordance with your organization's security standards after initial deployment. To learn more, see Managing Deployed Software Components.

Because vulnerabilities are regularly found in core open-source components such as DNS resolvers and the Linux Kernel, Zscaler recommends either patching or using new Zscaler-distributed VM images on a regular basis, or protecting App Connectors using firewall policies. Additionally, if you've installed the App Connector as a package, Zscaler recommends that you take similar precautions.

Some organizations choose to firewall or otherwise restrict outbound traffic to the internet from the data center. It is possible to deploy an App Connector in such an environment as long as the App Connector is able to reach all Zscaler data centers containing Public Service Edges for Private Access. For firewall configuration information for your deployment, see config.zscaler.com/private.zscaler.com/zpa (for the private.zscaler.com cloud) or config.zscaler.com/zpatwo.net/zpa (for the zpatwo.net cloud). To learn more, see Understanding Zscaler Cloud Names.

All Zscaler data centers containing Public Service Edges for Private Access must be allowed. A partial firewall configuration can result in connectivity problems for end users. Zscaler's policy is to provide a 90-day notice for activating additional IP CIDR ranges to provide organizations with sufficient opportunity for changing control policies.

Because the service enforces TLS certificate pinning for both client and server certificates, all forms of inline or man-in-the-middle TLS interception or inspection must be disabled. App Connectors do not function if the TLS certificates presented by the Public Service Edges or Private Service Edges do not cryptographically verify against Zscaler-trusted public keys.

By design, certificate verification is not configurable to maintain the integrity of the service. Ensure that *.prod.zpath.net is in your SSL bypass list for traffic originating from the App Connector. This is necessary for allowing the App Connector to resolve and reach Public Service Edges or Private Service Edges. If you are using OAuth 2.0, ensure that the OAuth server FQDN zpa-oauth.private.zscaler.com is in the allowlist, and user devices are allowed to make an outbound connection to the zpa-oauth.private.zscaler.com server. If you need to allowlist additional Zscaler IP addresses, see config.zscaler.com/private.zscaler.com/zpa (for the private.zscaler.com cloud) or config.zscaler.com/zpatwo.net/zpa (for the zpatwo.net cloud). To learn more, see Understanding Zscaler Cloud Names.

For Private Access integration with ZDX, App Connector firewall requirements must align with the respective ZDX configuration. You must configure the firewall to allow egress traffic on the TCP, UDP, and ICMP protocols. App Connectors must be able to egress traffic to port 443 for Zscaler Service Edge connections and the ports of all configured applications (i.e., ports that are configured in all application segments that are registered on the App Connector).
Step 2: Deploy the PRA Credential Agent on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9
To deploy the PRA credential agent:

Create a root Certificate Authority (CA) certificate that follows your corporate certificate creation SOP. A single private root CA is the shared trust anchor for App Connector and the credential agent.
Root CA (customer-managed) ├─ ZPA Enrollment CA (cm-appc-enrol – ZPA-owned key)(Created in Zscaler Admin Console) └─ Credential Agent leaf certificate (File you will be creating)
Private Access (ZPA) enrollment certificate signing requests (CSRs) are not usable as signing CAs by customers because the private key is not accessible.
Create a root CA private key on a secure admin system such as a domain controller, CA server, or an App Connector by entering the following command:
openssl genrsa -out rootCA.key 4096
Create a root CA certificate by entering the following command:
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key rootCA.key -sha256 -days 3650 \ -subj "/C=GB/O=Example/OU=ZPA-PKI/CN=Example ZPA Root CA" \ -out rootCA.crt
Outputs:
rootCA.key (secure, never upload)
rootCA.crt (distributed trust anchor)
Create an App Connector enrollment CSR:
Log in to Zscaler Admin Console.
From the navigation menu, go to Private Access > Private Infrastructure > Enrollment Certificates.
The Enrollment Certificates page appears.
See image.
On the Enrollment Certificates page, click Create CSR.
The Create CSR drawer opens.
In the Create CSR drawer:
Name: Enter a name and description that follows your naming convention (e.g., cm-appc-enrol).
Description: (Optional) Enter a description (e.g., credential agent).
Click Create.
Locate the certificate you created, and click the Download icon.
See image.
Sign the enrollment CSR as a CA certificate:
Open a text editor like Notepad.
Copy and paste the following into the text editor:
basicConstraints = critical,CA:TRUE,pathlen:0 keyUsage = critical, keyCertSign, cRLSign subjectKeyIdentifier = hash authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid,issuer
Save the file using the following name: enrollment_ca_ext.cnf
See image.
Sign the CSR by entering the following command:
If you are signing the CSR using the App Connector, move the cm-appc-enrol.csr and enrollment_ca_ext.cnf files to the admin /home directory on the App Connector server before you run the command.
openssl x509 -req -in cm-appc-enrol.csr \ -CA rootCA.crt -CAkey rootCA.key -CAcreateserial \ -out cm-appc-enrol.crt -days 1825 -sha256 \ -extfile enrollment_ca_ext.cnf
The following certificates are created: rootCA.crt and cm-appc-enrol.crt
Upload the newly created certificates:
Rename cm-appc-enrol.csr and enrollment_ca_ext.cnf to add a .txt extension to the end of the certificate name:
rootCA.crt.txt
cm-appc-enrol.crt.txt
Copy the contents from rootCA.crt.txt into cm-appc-enrol.crt.txt.
See image.
Rename both certificate files to remove the .txt extension.
In the Zscaler Admin Console, go to Private Access > Private Infrastructure > Enrollment Certificates.
Locate the cm-appc-enrol certificate, and click the Upload icon.
The Upload Signed Certificate drawer opens.
In the Upload Signed Certificate drawer:
Name: Add -root to the certificate name.
Certificate: Drag and drop the cm-appc-enrol.crt file from your system to upload it.
See image.
Click Upload.
The certificate is added to the table.
See image.
Deploy and configure App Connector:
Select the platform you want to use for the App Connector deployment.
Deploy the App Connector on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 (RHEL9).
Do not enroll the App Connector at this time.
In the Zscaler Admin Console, go to Private Access > Private Infrastructure > App Connector Groups.
The App Connector Groups page appears.
Click Add.
The Add page appears.
On the Add page, complete the fields as described in Configuring App Connector Groups. Make sure you select cm-appc-enrol from the Enrollment Certificate drop-down menu.
See image.
Click Save.
Go to Private Access > Private Infrastructure > App Connector Keys.
The App Connector Provisioning Keys page appears.
Click Add.
The App Connector Provisioning Key drawer opens.
In the App Connector Provisioning Keys drawer, complete the fields as described in Configuring App Connector Provisioning Keys. Make sure you set the following options:
App Connector Group: Select the App Connector group you previously created from the drop-down menu.
Signing Certificate: Select the cm-appc-enrol certificate from the drop-down menu.
Click Save.
Copy the provisioning key to use for enrolling the App Connector.
Log in locally to the deployed App Connector or from a secure machine that has PuTTY installed, use ssh to connect to the App Connector server.
If you are using PuTTY, make sure SSH is installed and enabled in the App Connector.
Perform the following commands to enroll your App Connector:
Stop running the zpa-connector service. If the provisioning key is not detected when the App Connector first starts, the App Connector is in a sleep cycle and looks for the key again every 24 hours.
$ sudo systemctl stop zpa-connector
Create a provisioning key file with 644 permissions at /opt/zscaler/var/provision_key. For example:
$ sudo touch /opt/zscaler/var/provision_key $ sudo chmod 644 /opt/zscaler/var/provision_key
Copy the provisioning key from the Zscaler Admin Console, paste it into the file, and save it. Use an editor, such as vi.
$ sudo vi /opt/zscaler/var/provision_key
If you are using vi, make sure it is in insert mode before you paste the key into the file.
If you are unfamiliar with the vi editor, you can also use the following echo and tee commands to paste in the provisioning key:
$ echo "<App Connector Provisioning Key>" | sudo tee /opt/zscaler/var/provision_key
Make sure that the key is within double quotes (").
Start the zpa-connector service.
$ sudo systemctl start zpa-connector
Verify the service status:
sudo systemctl status zpa-connector
In the Zscaler Admin Console, go to Private Access > Private Infrastructure > App Connectors.
Verify that the App Connector appears in the table and shows the following statuses:
Connection Health: Connected
Status: Enabled
Create a credential agent certificate (leaf).
Create a credential agent key on a secure admin system such as a domain controller, CA server, or an App Connector by entering the following command:
openssl genrsa -out cm-credagent.key 2048
Create the credential agent CSR with a Subject Alternative Name (SAR):
Open a text editor.
Review the following table to ensure you enter the correct information in the next step.

table: Your organization's two-letter country code (e.g., US).
The state or province where the server is located (e.g., Virginia).
The city where the server is located (e.g., Alexandria).
Your legal company name that is registered with your CA.
This identifies the specific service role (e.g., ZscalerCredentialAgent). Using this specific OU helps your internal PKI team (or Zscaler) categorize the certificate and apply the correct policies.
This is the primary identity of the credential agent host. It must match the FQDN of the App Connector server where the agent is installed.
The technical contact responsible for the certificate (e.g., infosec@yourcompany.com).

The FQDN of the Linux server where the credential agent is hosted. Even though the credential agent is co-located with the App Connector on the same Linux server, the certificate is used to secure communication and verify the identity of the agent. This should be the same value as the CN field.

blocks.item: Copy and paste the following into the text editor:

[ req ] default_bits = 2048 prompt = no default_md = sha256 distinguished_name = dn req_extensions = req_ext [ dn ] C = Enter Value ST = Enter Value L = Enter Value O = Enter Value OU = Enter Value CN = FQDN E = Enter Value [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = FQDN
Save the file using the following name: credagent_csr.cnf. Make sure you remove the .txt extension after saving the file.
Generate the CSR by entering the following commands:
openssl req -new -key cm-credagent.key \ -out cm-credagent.csr \ -config credagent_csr.cnf
Sign the CSR using the root credential agent certificate:
Open a text editor.
Copy the following information into the editor:
basicConstraints = critical,CA:FALSE keyUsage = critical, digitalSignature, keyEncipherment extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth subjectKeyIdentifier = hash authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid,issuer
Save the file using the following name: credagent_leaf_ext.cnf.
Sign the file by entering the following command:
openssl x509 -req -in cm-credagent.csr \ -CA rootCA.crt -CAkey rootCA.key -CAcreateserial \ -out cm-credagent.crt -days 825 -sha256 \ -extfile credagent_leaf_ext.cnf
Build the full chain (recommended) by entering the following command:
cat cm-credagent.crt rootCA.crt > credagent-fullchain.crt
Install and configure the credential agent:
Log in locally to the deployed App Connector or from a secure machine that has PuTTY installed, use ssh to connect to the App Connector server.
Enter the following command to download the credential agent onto the App Connector from the Zscaler cloud repository:
yum update -y yum install zpa-credential-agent -y
See image.
To verify that the installation was successful, enter the following command in the App Connector.
rpm -qa | grep zpa-credential-agent
A package with the current credential agent version should appear, as shown in the following example:
Create a folder to store the credential agent certification for the credential agent application to read:
After installing the credential agent application, create an app folder under /opt/zscaler/.
In the virtual serial console, navigate to the newly created folder: /opt/zscaler/app.
Create a folder hierarchy /app/config/certs using the following commands:
sudo mkdir config cd config/ sudo mkdir certs cd certs
Copy the rootCA.crt for the credential agent certificate, credential agent certificate, and credential agent key into the certs folder using the following commands:

cp rootCA.crt /opt/zscaler/app/config/certs/ cp cm-credagent.crt /opt/zscaler/app/config/certs/ cp cm-credagent.key /opt/zscaler/app/config/certs/ chmod 644 /opt/zscaler/app/config/certs/*.crt chmod 600 /opt/zscaler/app/config/certs/*.key
To verify that the certificates were copied, enter the following command on the App Connector console:
ls -l /opt/zscaler/app/config/certs
A message similar to the following should appear:
Install the AD LDAP certificate:
Install the AD LDAP certificate issuing CA into the App Connector's system trust using the command:
sudo cp rootADCA.crt /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/ sudo update-ca-trust
Make sure the name of the certificate is rootADCA.crt.
To verify that the certificate was installed on the App Connector's system trust, enter the following command on the App Connector console:
trust list
A list of all the certificates appears. Make sure the AD LDAP CA certificate is listed.
Configure the credential agent:
Create a JSON file named agent_cfg.json, and copy the following values into the file:

{ "server_cert_file_name": "config/certs/cm-credagent.crt", "server_private_key_file_name": "config/certs/cm-credagent.key", "client_ca_cert_file_name": "config/certs/rootCA.crt", "api_srvr_port": 9443, "api_srvr_host": "credagentclient.YourDomainName.com", "password_digits": "0123456789", "password_symbols": "!$%^&*()_+{}:@[];" }
Save the file.
Copy the agent_cfg.json file to /opt/zscaler/app/ using the following command:
sudo cp agent_cfg.json /opt/zscaler/app/
To verify that the JSON file was successfully copied, enter the following command on the App Connector console:
jq . /opt/zscaler/app/agent_cfg.json
A message similar to the following should appear:
Create a JSON file named idp_cfg.json, and copy the following values into the file:

[ { "IDP_zs_label": "ms-ad-ztpra", "IDP_type": 2, "host": "wins22s.example.com", "reconnect_count": 3, "conn_timeout_secs":5, "port": 636, "ldap_base": "DC=example,DC=com", "ldap_bindDN": "CN=service-account-name,DC=example,DC=com", "ldap_bindPass": "Enter Service Account Password", "ldap_derefAlias": 3, "passwords": { "password_length":15, "password_numDigits":4, "password_numSymbols":3, "password_noUpperCase":true, "password_allowRepeatChars":false } } ]
An LDAP service account is required to integrate with Active Directory. As a best practice, the service account should be restricted to resetting a password in respective organizational units.
Review the following table for the appropriate values in the file:

table: Enter a label that indicates whether you are using Microsoft Entra or Azure Active Directory.
Specify the IDP_type as 1 for Entra ID or 2 for Active Directory.
The hostname of the Entra or Active Directory server.
The number of times the PRA credential agent attempts to reconnect to Entra or Active Directory server before timing out.
The number of seconds before an attempted connection times out.
The port number for the Entra or Active Directory server.

The Base Distinguished Name (Base DN) that defines the starting point in your directory's hierarchy where the agent begins its search for users or objects. Only objects within or below this path are visible to the agent.

The Bind Distinguished Name, which is the full DN (identity) of the service account the agent uses to log in to the LDAP server. The agent binds using this account to gain the permissions needed to read user data or perform password operations.
The method for handling aliased objects when searching.
The total number of characters required for the password.
The minimum number of numerical digits (0–9) that must be included in the password.
The minimum number of special characters/symbols (e.g., ! @ #) required in the password.
When set to true, uppercase letters (A–Z) are not used or allowed in the password.
When set to false, the password cannot contain consecutive identical characters (e.g., aa or 11).

blocks.item: See example file.

[ { "IDP_zs_label": "ms-ad-sjc", "IDP_type": 2, "host": "ad-server1a-pdx12-autobot.mojito.local", "reconnect_count": 3, "port": 636, "ldap_base": "DC=example,DC=local", "ldap_bindDN": "CN=ServiceAccount,CN=Users,DC=example,DC=local", "ldap_bindPass": "AdminPasswd", “ldap_derefAlias”:3 "passwords": { "password_length":15, "password_numDigits":4, "password_numSymbols":3, "password_noUpperCase":true, "password_allowRepeatChars":false } }, { "IDP_zs_label": "entra-fra", "IDP_type": 1, "host": "https://graph.microsoft.com", "reconnect_count": 3, "port": 443, "entra_tenantID": "ccedasdas-664c-b5ed-758c6b6293de", "entra_clientID": "k809ond-a1s2-1234-8e2b-0da562947902", "entra_clientSecret": "q6tyu~8h7fdhXi5S09jhsyW-vIam1O.Zasghy6", "login_host": "https://login.microsoftonline.com" "passwords": { "password_length":15, "password_numDigits":4, "password_numSymbols":3, "password_noUpperCase":true, "password_allowRepeatChars":false } } ]
Save the file.

The idp_cfg.json file is automatically encrypted after the zpa-credential-agent service is started. The contents of this file cannot be decrypted. Therefore, it is recommended to securely store the service account credentials in a vault, as the idp_cfg.json file will need to be recreated if any configuration changes are required.
Copy the idp_cfg.json file to /opt/zscaler/app/ using the following command:
sudo cp idp_cfg.json /opt/zscaler/app/
To verify that the JSON file was successfully copied, enter the following command on the App Connector console:
jq . /opt/zscaler/app/idp_cfg.json
A message similar to the following should appear:
Configure an application segment:
In the Zscaler Admin Console, go to Private Access > Private Applications > Application Segments.

Step 3: Rotate Passwords and Onboard Accounts
The section describes how to create a password rotation policy, discover Active Directory and Entra ID accounts, and assign password and password pools to PRA application tiles.
Use a Password Rotation Policy
From the navigation menu, go to Zero Trust Browser > Credentials Management > Credentials Classes.
The Credential Classes page appears with a list of default policies that are available. You can add additional policies or edit the current ones.
Discover Accounts
From the navigation menu, go to Zero Trust Browser > Credentials Management > Privileged Credentials > Discovered.
Click Discover Credential.
The Discover Credentials drawer opens.
Click Add.
The Add Discovery Filter window appears.
In the Add Discovery Filter window:
Credential Provider: Select your newly onboarded credential provider.
Discovery filter: Enter the following query:
(&(objectclass=user)(SAMAccountName=SERVICEACCOUNTNAME*))
The SERVICEACCOUNTNAME value should reflect the service account that was created earlier in the deployment process.
Name: Enter a name for the filter.
See image.
Click Submit.
Click the Discovered tab.
Click the Refresh icon.
A list of discovered accounts appear.
Use Credential Pooling

If you use credential pooling with PRA, it groups multiple privileged credentials (RDP username/password, SSH key, VNC/RealVNC password) into a single pool and maps that pool to a privileged console via a Privileged Credentials policy using SAML/SCIM criteria. Users can launch a privileged console without entering credentials, and multiple users can access the same console concurrently with different pooled credentials. If all credentials in the pool are in use, new sessions are blocked until a credential is available.
To add a privileged credential pool:
From the navigation menu, go to Zero Trust Browser > Credentials Management > Credential Pools.
The Credential Pools page appears.
Click Add.
The Add Credential Pool drawer opens.
In the Add Credential Pool drawer:
Name: Enter a name for the credential pool.
Credential Type: Select a credential type for the pool.
If you are using Active Directory, select Username+Password for the credential type.
Privileged Credentials: Select the privileged credentials that you want to group together.
See image.
Click Save.
Import the Discovered Accounts and Other Options for the Credential Agent
From the navigation menu, go to Zero Trust Browser > Credentials Management > Privileged Credentials > Discovered.
Select all of the accounts you want to add to the application pool, and then click Import.
The Import Privileged Credentials page appears.
On the Import Privileged Credentials page:
Credential Class: Select the password rotation policy to use from the drop-down menu.
Credential Pool: If you added a credential pool, select the name of it from the drop-down menu.
See image.
Click Import.
Rotate the password(s) for the accounts because discovery does not provide the password value:
Select the Managed tab.
Select the checkbox next to all of the newly onboarded credentials, and click Rotate.
